problems.title: Pick the algorithm

parts.prompt: Grid where moving into a wall costs 1 and into an open cell 0:
Road network, non-negative travel times, one source:
Exchange rates; detect an arbitrage loop:

problems.solution: 0/1 weights → deque; non-negative → Dijkstra; negative cycles → Bellman–Ford.

problems.title: Run Dijkstra
problems.solution: dist = [0, 3, 1, 4]: 2 is reached via 3 (cost 3 beats 4), 4 via 2 (cost 4 beats 6). Delay = 4.

problems.title: Negative edge
problems.statement: Edges A→B 2, A→C 3, C→B −2. Dijkstra from A.
hints: Dijkstra settles B before seeing the C→B edge.
problems.solution: B (2) is popped before C (3) and treated as final; the route via C costs 1. Negative edges break the "settled is final" proof.

problems.title: Stops limit
problems.solution: Direct 500; with one stop 0→2→3 = 400; with two stops 0→1→2→3 = 300.

problems.title: The copy
problems.statement: Bellman–Ford for "at most k edges", relaxing in place (no copy), edges in the order 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, each costing 1, with k + 1 = 1 round.

parts.prompt: In-place dist(3) after the single round?
Correct answer with at most 1 edge?

hints: In-place relaxation chains edges within one round.
problems.solution: In place, the round relaxes 0→1, then 1→2 from the updated value, then 2→3: three edges in one round. Relaxing from the previous round's array keeps round i at ≤ i edges.

problems.title: Minimax

options: Kruskal with union-find until the corners connect

hints: Try 1 → 3 → 5 → 3 → 5 down the left column and along the bottom row.
problems.solution: 2: the route 1 → 3 → 5 → 3 → 5 (down the left column, then along the bottom row) has every step equal to 2, while the top-then-right route has a step of 3 (from 2 to 5). All three monotone-cost approaches work; step count is irrelevant.

problems.title: Overflow
problems.statement: In C++, dist initialised to INT_MAX, then if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]).

options: INT_MAX + w overflows (undefined; often negative), making unreachable nodes look close

problems.solution: Use long long with a large INF, or skip u when dist[u] == INF.

problems.title: Dense or sparse?

parts.prompt: Heap Dijkstra, E log V operations (millions, log₂ 2000 ≈ 11)?

hints: Compare E log V with V².
problems.solution: 44M versus 4M: on dense graphs the O(V²) array version wins. This is the same reasoning as choosing Prim over Kruskal for complete graphs.
